'''Erich Hüttenhain''' (26 January 1905 in [[Siegen]] &ndash; 1 December 1990 in [[Brühl (Rhineland)|Brühl]]) was a German academic [[mathematician]] and [[cryptography|cryptographer]] and considered a leading [[Cryptanalysis|cryptanalyst]] in the Third Reich.<ref name="Bauer2008">{{cite book|author=Friedrich L. Bauer|title=Historische Notizen zur Informatik|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tMsfBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA388|date=12 December 2008|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-540-85790-7|pages=388–}}</ref> He was Head of the cryptanalysis unit at OKW/Chi, the [[Cipher Department of the High Command of the Wehrmacht]].<ref name="Joyner2012">{{cite book|author=David Joyner|title=Coding Theory and Cryptography: From Enigma and Geheimschreiber to Quantum Theory|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TVvrCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA33|date=6 December 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-642-59663-6|pages=33}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://docs.google.com/folderview?id=0B_oIJbGCCNYeMGUxNzk0NWQtNzNhZi00YWVjLWI1NmItMzc2YWZiZGNjNjQ5&usp=drive_web|title=I-2 Interrogation of Erich Hüttenhain and Dr Fricke at Flensburg  |page = 1|date=21 May 1945 |website=Google Drive |access-date=24 July 2016}}</ref>

==Life==
Hüttenhain was the son of a [[Rector (ecclesiastical)|conrector]] and studied after the high school diploma ({{langx|de|Abitur}}) 1924 in [[Siegen-Wittgenstein|Siegen]] at the [[University of Marburg]], the [[Goethe University Frankfurt|Johann Wolfgang Goethe-University Frankfurt]] and the [[University of Münster]]. He studied mathematics with [[Heinrich Behnke]] and astronomy at Münster. There he was assistant to {{ill|Martin Lindow|de|Martin Lindow (Astronom)}} (1880–1967), who was director of the observatory at Münster. In 1933, at the University of Münster, he took his examination for promotion of [[Doctor of Philosophy|Dr. phil.]] in astronomy under Lindow with the thesis titled: ''Spatial infinitesimal orbits around the libration points in the straight-line case of the (3 + 1) bodies''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hüttenhain |first1=E. |title=Räumliche infinitesimale Bahnen um die Librationspunkte im Geradlinien‐Fall der (3+1)‐Körper. |journal=Astronomische Nachrichten |date=January 1933 |volume=250 |issue=18 |pages=297–316 |doi=10.1002/asna.19332501802}}</ref>

==Military career==
In 1936, he was sent to the cipher bureau of the OKW [[Cipher Department of the High Command of the Wehrmacht|OKW/Chi]] under the director [[Wilhelm Fenner]]. Erich Hüttenhain had an interest in [[Maya civilization|Mayan chronology]] which led him to cryptology and thus to OKW/CHi. As a recruitment test, Fenner had sent him a message which had been enciphered with a private cipher. Hüttenhain duly deciphered it and was accepted as a possible cryptanalyst.<ref>Bauer Historical notes on computer science, Springer 2009 S.388, with photo</ref> At OKW/Chi he was employed as a specialist to build a cryptanalytic research unit, and later he was most recently Executive Council Head of group IV Analytical [[cryptanalysis]].

During his time in OKW/Chi he succeeded, among other things, in the deciphering of the Japanese [[Purple (cipher machine)|Purple]] cipher machine ([[William F. Friedman|William Frederick Friedman]])<ref>Leiberich, Scientific American, June 1999 and plus there is to Leiberich in Germany but no documents</ref> He and his staff <ref>"Cipher Department of the High Command of the Wehrmacht#German Mathematicians Who Worked at OKW" Wikipedia: The Free Encyclopedia. Wikimedia Foundation, Inc. 8 July 2016. Web. 11 July 2016.</ref> also temporarily succeeded in deciphering American [[Rotor machine|rotary machines]], such as the M 138 A and the [[M-209]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.heise.de/tp/artikel/18/18371/1.html |title=Als deutscher Code-Knacker im Zweiten Weltkrieg (As a German code breaker during World War II) |last=Schmeh |first=Klaus |publisher= Telepolis, Heise Zeitschriften Verlag |date=23 September 2004 |website=Heise Online|access-date=2019-01-18}}</ref> in [[North Africa]]. Later in the war, when the allies [[Allied invasion of Italy|invaded]] Italy, the allies learned in turn by deciphering Italian ciphers that their later systems, e.g. among others the [[SIGABA]] designed by Friedman, had not been broken and around that time, Hüttenhain had no more major successes.

After [[World War II]], being a high value target, he was taken by [[TICOM]] to the USA to be interrogated.<ref name="Bamford2008">{{cite book|author=James Bamford|title=Body Of Secrets|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E2hnNp8G9wAC|date=4 September 2008|publisher=Random House|isbn=978-1-4070-0920-9|page=17|quote=It is almost certain that no major cryptoanalytic successes were achieved without his knowledge.}}</ref> For the Americans, he built a machine (which was already used by the Germans during World War II) that deciphered the Russian rotor machine encryption.<ref>Leiberich, loc.</ref> He also created reports on the successes of the Germans on cryptographic territory during World War II (as deciphering the French naval codes, the Polish diplomat cipher and the security of the [[Enigma machine|Enigma]]).

==Gehlen organisation==
After his return he founded in 1947 the "Study Group for Scientific Investigation" ({{langx|de|Studiengesellschaft für wissenschaftliche Arbeiten}})<ref>{{Citation |last=Wala |first=Michael |contribution=Digest of Papers: Germany and Intelligence Organizations: The Last Fifty Years in Review |year=1999 |title=Annual Conference 1999, 18–20 June, Tutzing, Germany |publisher=International Intelligence History Association |contribution-url=http://intelligence-history.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/10/IIHA-Conf-1999-report.pdf |page=3}}</ref> within the [[Gehlen Organization]], which laid the foundation for the subsequent formation of the German Central Office for Encryption ({{langx|de|Zentralstelle für das Chiffrierwesen) (ZfCh)}}, a unit of the German Federal Intelligence Service ({{langx|de|Bundesnachrichtendienst}}).<ref name="AidWiebes2013">{{cite book|author1=Matthew M. Aid|author2=Cees Wiebes|title=Secrets of Signals Intelligence During the Cold War: From Cold War to Globalization|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eeL9AQAAQBAJ&pg=PA160|date=5 November 2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-28098-7|page=160}}</ref><ref name="Adams2009">{{cite book|author=Jefferson Adams|title=Historical Dictionary of German Intelligence|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gnEWm4kC844C&pg=PA517|date=1 September 2009|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-6320-0|pages=517}}</ref> His pseudonym in the Gehlen organization was Erich Hammerschmidt.<ref>Bauer, Historical notes on computer science, S.&nbsp;388</ref> In the first official cryptographic service of the Federal Government, the Unit 114 in the Foreign Ministry, headed by Adolf Paschke<ref name="Bauer2006">{{cite book|author=Friedrich L. Bauer|title=Decrypted Secrets: Methods and Maxims of Cryptology|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hfWTDr_bvMwC&pg=PA415|date=24 November 2006|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-48121-8|page=415|chapter=19.4.1.2|quote=Of Per S Z}}</ref> founded in 1950, he was the chair of the Scientific Advisory Board, along with Kurt Selchow, Rudolf Schauffler, and Heinz Kuntze, some of the best cryptologists in Germany.<ref name="AidWiebes2013" /> During 1956–1970 he served as Deputy Director of the Central Office for Encryption where initially Wilhelm Göing and 1972 [[Otto Leiberich]] was his successor. One of the objectives of Hüttenhain was that in contrast to his experiences in the [[Nazi Germany|Third Reich]] where numerous independent cipher bureaux were spread throughout the Reich, all threads for evaluating cryptographic procedures were now to be integrated into a single office.

In 1926 he was a founding fellow of the Frankfurt [[Burschenschaft]] Arminia .<ref>H. de Rouet: 150 years of Frankfurt-Leipziger Burschenschaft Arminia, Frankfurt 2010, p 324</ref>

Hüttenhain left a posthumous manuscript he wrote in about 1970 and in which he reports on his experience as a cryptologist.<ref>Monographs in the field of cryptology. A copy is in the [[Bavarian State Library]]. [[Friedrich L. Bauer|Friedrich Bauer]] referenced it in his book Historical notes on computer science, Springer 2009 S.&nbsp;389ff</ref>
